---
title: "Snakemake-ify: answers"
description: "Worked solutions for the Snakemake-ify exercises, with what each legacy script got wrong and how the rules fix it."
code-annotations: below
---

All solution files are in `answers/snakemakeify/` in the course repository:

```
answers/snakemakeify/
  config.yaml          every setting that was a variable at the top of a script
  common.smk           reads the samplesheet; sample lists; wildcard constraints
  rules/*.smk          the rules for each exercise (fastqc, align, filter, peaks,
                       sweep, qc, overlap, plot, ttseq)
  scripts/             the Python and R scripts, edited for script:
  ex1.smk ... ex9.smk  one runnable Snakefile per exercise
  Snakefile            exercise S10: everything in one file
```

Each `exN.smk` loads the config, includes `common.smk` and the rule files it
needs, and has its own `rule all`. Run them from your working folder (the one
with the `data` link), for example
`snakemake -s ~/snakemake-course/answers/snakemakeify/ex4.smk -c 4`.

Every number on this page comes from running the legacy scripts and these
solutions on the course data, with Snakemake 8.27.1 on a 4-core machine.

## Shared setup: `common.smk`

Exercise S1 is the first place you need the sample list, so here is the file
every exercise includes.

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/common.smk"}
# Shared by every exercise Snakefile: read the samplesheet once and
# build the sample lists the rules need.
import pandas as pd

DATA = config["data"]  # <1>

sheet = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/samplesheet.txt", sep="\t", dtype=str,
                    keep_default_na=False)  # <2>
sheet["sample"] = sheet[config["fileNamesFrom"]].agg("_".join, axis=1)  # <3>
sheet = sheet.set_index("sample", drop=False)

SAMPLES = sheet.index.tolist()
CONTROLS = sorted(set(sheet["Control"]) - {"NA"})  # <4>
PEAK_SAMPLES = [s for s in SAMPLES if s not in CONTROLS]
TARGETS = sorted(set(sheet.loc[PEAK_SAMPLES, "Target"]))


def reps_of(target):
    """Peak-calling samples of one target, in samplesheet order."""
    return [s for s in PEAK_SAMPLES if sheet.loc[s, "Target"] == target]


wildcard_constraints:  # <5>
    sample="|".join(SAMPLES),
    target="|".join(TARGETS),
    q=r"[0-9.]+",
```
1. The data folder comes from `config.yaml` (`data: "data"`), relative to where
   you run Snakemake. This replaces `DATA=~/snakemake-course/data` at the top
   of every legacy script: you change it once, or on the command line with
   `--config data=/path/to/data`.
2. `keep_default_na=False` keeps the text `NA` in the `Control` column as the
   string `"NA"`. Without it pandas turns it into a missing value and
   `control != "NA"` is always true.
3. Sample names are built from the samplesheet columns listed in
   `fileNamesFrom`, the same way the lab pipelines do it. The legacy scripts
   typed the list three times (01, 02, 03) and built it a fourth way in 04.
4. A control is any sample named in someone's `Control` column. The legacy
   script decided by name (`target == input*`); this works for an IgG control
   too.
5. Constraining `{sample}` to the real sample names stops a pattern like
   `{sample}_q{q}_peaks.narrowPeak` from matching in odd ways, and turns a typo
   into a clear error.

## Exercise S1: FastQC {#ex-s1}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/fastqc.smk"}
# Exercise 1: 01_fastqc.sh
rule fastqc:
    input:
        f"{DATA}/fastq/{{sample}}.fastq.gz",  # <1>
    output:
        html="results/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html",  # <2>
        zip="results/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.zip",
    log:
        "results/logs/fastqc/{sample}.log",
    shell:
        "fastqc --quiet --outdir results/fastqc {input} > {log} 2>&1"
```
1. An f-string, so `{DATA}` is filled in by Python and `{{sample}}` (doubled
   braces) stays as the Snakemake wildcard `{sample}`.
2. FastQC decides its own output names: `<fastq name without .fastq.gz>_fastqc.html`
   and `.zip`. The rule has to declare exactly those, or Snakemake reports
   missing output after the job finishes.

`ex1.smk` adds the target:

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/ex1.smk (excerpt)"}
rule all:
    input:
        expand("results/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html", sample=SAMPLES),  # <1>
```
1. `expand()` with `SAMPLES` replaces the `for s in $SAMPLES` loop. Snakemake
   works backwards from these ten file names to ten `fastqc` jobs.

**What the legacy script got wrong.** Nothing serious. The skip check looks
at the HTML only, so a run killed between writing the HTML and the zip would
be skipped next time. Snakemake records a job as finished only when it ends
without error and all its outputs exist, and it marks outputs of an
interrupted job as incomplete so they are redone.

**Check.** `snakemake -s ex1.smk -n` shows 11 jobs (10 `fastqc`, 1 `all`).
`fastqc_data.txt` and `summary.txt` inside each zip are identical to the
legacy ones for all ten samples.

## Exercise S2: Index and align {#ex-s2}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/align.smk"}
# Exercise 2: 02_align.sh
rule reference:
    input:
        f"{DATA}/reference/chr8_course.fa.gz",
    output:
        fa="results/index/chr8_course.fa",
        fai="results/index/chr8_course.fa.fai",  # <1>
    shell:
        "gunzip -c {input} > {output.fa} && samtools faidx {output.fa}"


rule bowtie2_index:
    input:
        rules.reference.output.fa,  # <2>
    output:
        multiext("results/index/chr8_course",
                 ".1.bt2", ".2.bt2", ".3.bt2", ".4.bt2", ".rev.1.bt2", ".rev.2.bt2"),  # <3>
    params:
        prefix="results/index/chr8_course",
    log:
        "results/logs/bowtie2_index.log",
    threads: 4
    shell:
        "bowtie2-build --threads {threads} {input} {params.prefix} > {log} 2>&1"


rule align:
    input:
        fq=f"{DATA}/fastq/{{sample}}.fastq.gz",
        index=rules.bowtie2_index.output,  # <4>
    output:
        bam="results/align/{sample}.bam",
        bai="results/align/{sample}.bam.bai",
    params:
        prefix=rules.bowtie2_index.params.prefix,
    log:
        "results/logs/align/{sample}.bowtie2.log",
    threads: 4  # <5>
    shell:
        "bowtie2 -p {threads} -x {params.prefix} -U {input.fq} 2> {log}"  # <6>
        " | samtools sort -@ 2 -o {output.bam} -"
        " && samtools index {output.bam}"
```
1. The `.fai` is now a declared output. In the legacy version it was made
   "for later" and used by `07_overlap.sh` without saying so. Here any rule that
   needs it lists it as an input (S7 does).
2. `rules.reference.output.fa` refers to the other rule's output by name, so
   the path is typed once.
3. All six index files are outputs. If one is missing, Snakemake reruns the
   index. The legacy check looked for `chr8_course.1.bt2` only: with just that
   file present, `02_align.sh` skipped the index, bowtie2 failed for all ten
   samples, and the script still exited with status 0.
4. The align jobs depend on the whole index, so they wait for it, and a new
   index makes them out of date.
5. `threads:` replaces `THREADS=4`. On a laptop with `-c 2`, Snakemake lowers
   it to 2 and `{threads}` follows.
6. Snakemake runs every `shell:` with `set -euo pipefail`. If bowtie2 fails,
   the pipe fails, the job fails, and Snakemake deletes the half-written BAM.
   The legacy script had no `pipefail`, so only `samtools sort` decided
   whether the step "worked".

**Check.** 13 jobs. Record counts match the legacy BAMs for every sample
(HCT116_CTCF_1: 28634, HCT116_H3K27ac_2: 210899). The files are not
byte-for-byte identical: with `-p 4` bowtie2 writes reads in the order its
threads finish, so reads at the same position can be sorted in a different
order. Sorted, the records are identical (`samtools view x.bam | sort | md5sum`).

## Exercise S3: One script, many outputs {#ex-s3}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/filter.smk"}
# Exercise 3: 03_filter.sh
rule filter_reads:
    input:
        bam="results/align/{sample}.bam",
        blacklist=f"{DATA}/reference/blacklist.bed.gz",
    output:
        temp("results/filter/{sample}.noBL.bam"),  # <1>
    params:
        mapq=config["filter"]["mapq"],  # <2>
    shell:
        "samtools view -b -q {params.mapq} {input.bam}"
        " | bedtools intersect -v -abam stdin -b {input.blacklist} > {output}"


rule markdup:
    input:
        "results/filter/{sample}.noBL.bam",
    output:
        bam="results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam",
        bai="results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam.bai",
    log:
        "results/logs/markdup/{sample}.log",
    shell:
        "samtools markdup -r {input} {output.bam} 2> {log}"
        " && samtools index {output.bam}"


rule flagstat:  # <3>
    input:
        "results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam",
    output:
        "results/filter/{sample}.flagstat.txt",
    shell:
        "samtools flagstat {input} > {output}"


rule bigwig:
    input:
        bam="results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam",
        bai="results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam.bai",  # <4>
    output:
        "results/tracks/{sample}.bw",
    params:
        binsize=config["bigwig"]["binsize"],
        extend_reads=config["bigwig"]["extend"],  # <5>
    log:
        "results/logs/bigwig/{sample}.log",
    threads: 4
    shell:
        "bamCoverage -b {input.bam} -o {output} --normalizeUsing CPM"
        " --binSize {params.binsize} --extendReads {params.extend_reads} -p {threads} 2> {log}"
```
1. `temp()` replaces `rm $s.q$MAPQ.bam $s.noBL.bam`. Snakemake deletes the file
   once every job that needs it has finished. The MAPQ-filtered BAM is gone
   entirely: it goes straight into bedtools through a pipe.
2. `MAPQ=30` is now `filter: mapq: 30` in `config.yaml`. Because it is a
   `params:` value, changing it in the config makes Snakemake rerun this rule
   and everything downstream.
3. One rule per thing a later step needs. The legacy loop wrote six files per
   sample behind one skip check on `$s.filt.bam`: if `bamCoverage` failed, the
   next run skipped that sample and the bigWig never appeared. Here a missing
   bigWig is one `bigwig` job.
4. bamCoverage needs the index but does not name it on the command line. List
   it as an input anyway, so the job never starts before `samtools index` is done.
5. A params name cannot be `extend` (Snakemake reserves it; you get
   "extend is reserved for internal use"), hence `extend_reads`.

**Check.** 53 jobs from scratch. The ten flagstat files and the ten bigWigs are
byte-for-byte identical to the legacy ones. HCT116_CTCF_1 keeps 24453 of its
28634 reads. The filtered BAMs have the same read counts, but for 8 of the 10
samples a few different reads survive: when duplicates tie, `samtools markdup`
keeps the first one it sees, and that depends on the bowtie2 thread order from
S2. The kept reads sit at the same positions, which is why the bigWigs, and in
S4 the peaks, are identical.

## Exercise S4: Peaks with a control {#ex-s4}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/peaks.smk"}
# Exercise 4: 04_call_peaks.sh
def macs3_inputs(wildcards):  # <1>
    """Treatment BAM, plus the control BAM named in the samplesheet."""
    inputs = {"treatment": f"results/filter/{wildcards.sample}.filt.bam"}
    control = sheet.loc[wildcards.sample, "Control"]
    if control != "NA":
        inputs["control"] = f"results/filter/{control}.filt.bam"
    return inputs


def macs3_options(wildcards, input):  # <2>
    if "control" in input.keys():
        return f"-c {input.control} {config['macs3']['with_control']}"
    return config["macs3"]["no_control"]


rule call_peaks:
    input:
        unpack(macs3_inputs),  # <3>
    output:
        peaks="results/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak",
        summits="results/peaks/{sample}_summits.bed",
        xls="results/peaks/{sample}_peaks.xls",
    params:
        gsize=config["macs3"]["gsize"],
        qvalue=config["macs3"]["qvalue"],
        options=macs3_options,
    log:
        "results/logs/macs3/{sample}.log",
    shell:
        "macs3 callpeak -t {input.treatment} {params.options} -f BAM"
        " -g {params.gsize} -q {params.qvalue}"
        " -n {wildcards.sample} --outdir results/peaks 2> {log}"
```
1. The input function does what the `while read ... control` loop did: look up
   the sample's row and find its control by name. The difference is that
   Snakemake calls it while building the DAG, so the control BAM becomes a real
   dependency. Delete `results/filter/HCT116_input-CTCF_2.filt.bam` and
   Snakemake remakes it before calling peaks on HCT116_CTCF_2. The legacy script
   would have run MACS3 and failed.
2. A params function can take `input` as well as `wildcards`. ChIP gets
   `-c control` plus the ChIP options, DNase the cut-site options. Both strings
   live in `config.yaml`.
3. `unpack()` turns the returned dict into named inputs, so the shell command
   can use `{input.treatment}` and `{input.control}`.

**Which samples get peaks.** `PEAK_SAMPLES` (from `common.smk`) is every
sample that is not someone's control. `rule all` in `ex4.smk` asks for
`expand("results/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak", sample=PEAK_SAMPLES)`.

**Check.** 39 jobs, 6 `call_peaks`. All six `_peaks.narrowPeak` and
`_summits.bed` files are byte-for-byte identical to the legacy ones: 24 and 64
CTCF peaks, 138 and 141 H3K27ac, 223 and 217 DNase. (The `.xls` files differ
only in the command line MACS3 writes into their header.)

## Exercise S5: A parameter sweep {#ex-s5}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/sweep.smk"}
# Exercise 5: 05_qvalue_sweep.sh
SWEEP_SAMPLES = reps_of(config["sweep"]["target"])
QVALUES = config["sweep"]["qvalues"]  # <1>


rule sweep_call:
    input:
        treatment="results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam",
        control=lambda wc: f"results/filter/{sheet.loc[wc.sample, 'Control']}.filt.bam",  # <2>
    output:
        "results/sweep/{sample}_q{q}_peaks.narrowPeak",  # <3>
    params:
        gsize=config["macs3"]["gsize"],
        options=config["macs3"]["with_control"],
    log:
        "results/logs/sweep/{sample}_q{q}.log",
    shell:
        "macs3 callpeak -t {input.treatment} -c {input.control} {params.options} -f BAM"
        " -g {params.gsize} -q {wildcards.q}"
        " -n {wildcards.sample}_q{wildcards.q} --outdir results/sweep 2> {log}"


rule sweep_counts:
    input:
        expand("results/sweep/{sample}_q{q}_peaks.narrowPeak",
               sample=SWEEP_SAMPLES, q=QVALUES),  # <4>
    output:
        "results/sweep/sweep_counts.tsv",
    run:  # <5>
        # expand() loops over q fastest, so this matches the input order
        labels = [(s, q) for s in SWEEP_SAMPLES for q in QVALUES]
        with open(output[0], "w") as out:
            out.write("sample\tqvalue\tn_peaks\n")
            for (s, q), path in zip(labels, input):
                with open(path) as fh:
                    n = sum(1 for _ in fh)
                out.write(f"{s}\t{q}\t{n}\n")
```
1. The q-values are strings in `config.yaml` (`["0.05", "0.01", "0.001", "0.0001"]`),
   so the file names use exactly that text. To try a fifth cutoff, add it to
   the list: only the new jobs run.
2. The control comes from the samplesheet, as in S4. This is the bug in the
   legacy script: `CONTROL=HCT116_input-CTCF_1` was used for both replicates,
   but the samplesheet pairs HCT116_CTCF_2 with HCT116_input-CTCF_2.
3. `{q}` is a wildcard like `{sample}`. One rule covers the whole sweep, and
   the `[0-9.]+` constraint in `common.smk` keeps it from swallowing part of the
   sample name.
4. Two lists in one `expand()` give every combination: 2 samples x 4 q-values
   = 8 files, so 8 `sweep_call` jobs.
5. A short `run:` block (Python inside the rule) is enough for a table this
   small. `input` and `output` are the same objects as in `shell:`.

**Check.** 24 jobs from scratch: 8 `sweep_call`, `sweep_counts`, and only the
alignment and filtering the sweep needs (CTCF reps and their two controls).
The HCT116_CTCF_1 rows match the legacy table. The HCT116_CTCF_2 rows do not:

```
sample          qvalue  legacy  snakemake
HCT116_CTCF_2   0.05    66      67
HCT116_CTCF_2   0.01    62      64
HCT116_CTCF_2   0.001   57      60
HCT116_CTCF_2   0.0001  54      55
```

The legacy sweep called replicate 2 against replicate 1's input. The q 0.01
row should equal the 64 peaks from S4, which used the same settings, and only
the Snakemake version does. Because the legacy sweep and peak scripts each
had their own copy of the control choice, they drifted apart. With one
samplesheet lookup they cannot.

## Exercise S6: A Python script that globs {#ex-s6}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/qc.smk"}
# Exercise 6: 06_qc_summary.py
rule qc_summary:
    input:
        bams=expand("results/filter/{sample}.filt.bam", sample=SAMPLES),  # <1>
        flagstats=expand("results/filter/{sample}.flagstat.txt", sample=SAMPLES),
        peaks=expand("results/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak", sample=PEAK_SAMPLES),  # <2>
    output:
        "results/qc/qc_summary.tsv",
    params:
        samples=SAMPLES,  # <3>
        peak_samples=PEAK_SAMPLES,
    script:
        "../scripts/qc_summary.py"  # <4>
```
1. The `glob("*.filt.bam")` is now an explicit list. Snakemake knows the
   inputs before it runs anything, so it can make them first. The glob used
   whatever was in the folder: a sample whose filtering failed simply had no
   row, and a stale BAM from an old run would have got one.
2. Peak files are inputs too. The legacy script checked `os.path.exists(peaks)`
   and wrote `NA` if the file was not there, so running it before
   `04_call_peaks.sh` (or after MACS3 failed for one sample) gave a table with
   NA in it and exit status 0. Here a missing peak file means the rule waits for
   `call_peaks`, or stops with an error.
3. The script still needs to know which file is which sample. `params:` passes
   the names in the same order as the inputs.
4. A `script:` path is relative to the file the rule is in (`rules/`), hence `../`.

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/scripts/qc_summary.py"}
"""One QC table for all samples: reads after filtering, peaks, FRiP.

Called by the qc_summary rule with script:, so every file name comes
from the rule (snakemake.input, snakemake.params, snakemake.output).
"""
import subprocess

samples = snakemake.params.samples  # <1>
peak_files = dict(zip(snakemake.params.peak_samples, snakemake.input.peaks))

rows = []
for sample, bam, flagstat in zip(samples, snakemake.input.bams,
                                 snakemake.input.flagstats):
    # first line of flagstat is "<n> + 0 in total ..."
    with open(flagstat) as fh:
        n_reads = int(fh.readline().split()[0])

    peaks = peak_files.get(sample)
    if peaks is None:
        n_peaks, frip = "NA", "NA"   # a control: no peaks by design  # <2>
    else:
        with open(peaks) as fh:
            n_peaks = sum(1 for _ in fh)
        out = subprocess.run(["samtools", "view", "-c", "-L", peaks, bam],
                             capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        frip = f"{int(out.stdout) / n_reads:.4f}"

    rows.append((sample, n_reads, n_peaks, frip))

with open(snakemake.output[0], "w") as out:  # <3>
    out.write("sample\treads_filtered\tn_peaks\tfrip\n")
    for row in sorted(rows):
        out.write("\t".join(str(x) for x in row) + "\n")
```
1. `snakemake` is an object Snakemake puts into the script. No imports, no
   `argparse`, no paths.
2. `NA` now means one thing only: the sample is a control. In the legacy script
   it also meant "peaks missing for any reason".
3. Sorting by sample name keeps the row order of the legacy table (which came
   from the sorted glob), so the two files can be compared with `cmp`.

**Check.** 50 jobs from scratch. `results/qc/qc_summary.tsv` is byte-for-byte
identical to `legacy/qc_summary.tsv`. FRiP ranges from 0.0447 (HCT116_CTCF_1)
to 0.5327 (HCT116_H3K27ac_1).

## Exercise S7: Overlaps and a file that lies {#ex-s7}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/overlap.smk"}
# Exercise 7: 07_overlap.sh
rule consensus_peaks:
    input:
        lambda wc: expand("results/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak",
                          sample=reps_of(wc.target)),  # <1>
    output:
        "results/overlap/{target}_consensus.bed",
    params:
        rep1=lambda wc, input: input[0],  # <2>
        others=lambda wc, input: input[1:],
    shell:
        # replicate 1 peaks that overlap a peak in any other replicate
        "bedtools intersect -u -a {params.rep1} -b {params.others} > {output}"  # <3>


rule ctcf_rad21_overlap:
    input:
        ctcf="results/overlap/CTCF_consensus.bed",
        rad21=f"{DATA}/peaks/RAD21_ENCFF391AAM.bed.gz",
    output:
        "results/overlap/CTCF_with_RAD21.bed",
    shell:
        "bedtools intersect -u -a {input.ctcf} -b {input.rad21} > {output}"


rule ctcf_summit_windows:
    input:
        summits=lambda wc: f"results/peaks/{reps_of('CTCF')[0]}_summits.bed",
        fai=rules.reference.output.fai,  # <4>
    output:
        "results/overlap/CTCF_summits_200bp.bed",
    shell:
        "bedtools slop -b 100 -g {input.fai} -i {input.summits} > {output}"


rule overlap_counts:
    input:
        expand("results/overlap/{target}_consensus.bed", target=TARGETS),
        rules.ctcf_rad21_overlap.output,
        rules.ctcf_summit_windows.output,
    output:
        "results/overlap/counts.txt",
    shell:
        "wc -l {input} > {output}"
```
1. `{target}` is a wildcard that is not a sample. The input function asks the
   samplesheet for that target's replicates, so the targets and the
   `HCT116_${t}_1` / `_2` file names are no longer typed in.
2. Shell placeholders cannot slice a list (`{input[1:]}` does not work), so
   the first replicate and the rest go through `params:` functions.
3. With two replicates this is the legacy command exactly. With three it keeps
   rep 1 peaks found in either other replicate, which is a looser rule than
   "in all replicates"; RegPipe's `consensus_peaks` shows a stricter version.
4. The `.fai` is an input, made by the `reference` rule from S2. In the legacy
   version it was a side effect of `02_align.sh`.

**The file that lies.** In the legacy script, `bedtools ... > overlap/X.bed`
creates `X.bed` before bedtools runs. If bedtools fails (peaks not called yet,
or the `.fai` missing), the empty file stays, and the `if [ ! -f ... ]` check
treats it as done from then on. Running `07_overlap.sh` in an empty folder,
then copying in the peaks and the `.fai` and running it again, gives 0 lines
in all five files both times. Snakemake prevents this twice: it never starts a
job before its inputs exist, and when a job fails it deletes that job's
outputs, so a later run tries again.

**Check.** 45 jobs from scratch. All five BED files are byte-for-byte
identical to the legacy ones: 24 CTCF consensus peaks, 19 of them with a
RAD21 peak, 127 H3K27ac and 198 DNase consensus peaks, 24 summit windows.

## Exercise S8: An R figure with hard-coded files {#ex-s8}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/plot.smk"}
# Exercise 8: 08_locus_plot.R
rule locus_plot:
    input:
        bigwigs=expand("results/tracks/{sample}.bw", sample=PEAK_SAMPLES),  # <1>
        consensus=expand("results/overlap/{target}_consensus.bed", target=TARGETS),
        rad21=f"{DATA}/peaks/RAD21_ENCFF391AAM.bed.gz",
    output:
        pdf="results/figures/MYC_locus.pdf",
        tsv="results/figures/MYC_locus_CTCF_peaks.tsv",
    params:
        track_names=PEAK_SAMPLES,  # <2>
        peak_names=TARGETS,
        chrom=config["locus"]["chrom"],  # <3>
        start=config["locus"]["start"],
        end=config["locus"]["end"],
    log:
        "results/logs/locus_plot.log",
    script:
        "../scripts/locus_plot.R"
```
1. The six `bigwigs <- c(CTCF_1 = "tracks/...", ...)` lines become one
   `expand()`. A new sample in the samplesheet shows up in the figure without
   touching the R code.
2. Labels travel with the files, in the same order.
3. The region is in `config.yaml` (`locus: chrom, start, end`), not in the code.

The changed lines of the R script (the plotting code is the same as the legacy
version):

```{.r filename="answers/snakemakeify/scripts/locus_plot.R (top)"}
log <- file(snakemake@log[[1]], open = "wt")  # <1>
sink(log, type = "message")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicRanges)
  library(rtracklayer)
})

p <- snakemake@params
region <- GRanges(p$chrom, IRanges(p$start, p$end))  # <2>

bigwigs   <- setNames(unlist(snakemake@input$bigwigs), unlist(p$track_names))  # <3>
consensus <- setNames(unlist(snakemake@input$consensus), unlist(p$peak_names))
```
1. Messages and warnings go to the rule's log file instead of the terminal.
2. `snakemake@params` is a list with the names from the rule.
3. A named input with several files comes into R as a list. `unlist()` makes it
   a character vector; `setNames()` gives it the labels so the rest of the
   script (which loops over `names(signal)`) did not have to change. The
   output paths further down are `snakemake@output$pdf` and
   `snakemake@output$tsv`, and the RAD21 file is `snakemake@input$rad21`
   instead of the `~/snakemake-course/...` path.

**Check.** 49 jobs from scratch. `MYC_locus_CTCF_peaks.tsv` is byte-for-byte
identical to the legacy one (one CTCF consensus peak in chr8:127.3-127.8 Mb).
The PDF has the same six tracks and four peak rows; it is not byte-identical
because PDFs store their creation time, and the track labels are now the full
sample names.

## Exercise S9: TT-seq over enhancers {#ex-s9}

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/rules/ttseq.smk"}
# Exercise 9: 09_ttseq_enhancers.R
TT = config["ttseq"]


wildcard_constraints:
    rep=r"\d+",
    strand="|".join(TT["strands"]),


rule ttseq_signal:
    input:
        bigwig=f"{DATA}/{TT['bigwig']}",  # <1>
        enhancers=f"{DATA}/{TT['enhancers']}",
    output:
        "results/ttseq/rep{rep}_{strand}.tsv",  # <2>
    log:
        "results/logs/ttseq/rep{rep}_{strand}.log",
    script:
        "../scripts/ttseq_signal.R"


rule ttseq_tables:
    input:
        expand("results/ttseq/rep{rep}_{strand}.tsv",
               rep=TT["reps"], strand=TT["strands"]),  # <3>
    output:
        reps=expand("results/ttseq/ttseq_enhancers_rep{rep}.tsv", rep=TT["reps"]),  # <4>
        combined="results/ttseq/ttseq_enhancers_all.tsv",
    params:
        reps=TT["reps"],
        strands=TT["strands"],
    log:
        "results/logs/ttseq/tables.log",
    script:
        "../scripts/ttseq_tables.R"
```
1. The config holds the file pattern `geo/TTseq_HCT116_{rep}_{strand}.bw`.
   The value is pasted into the f-string, so its braces survive as wildcards.
   This replaces `paste0("TTseq_HCT116_", rep, "_", strand, ".bw")`.
2. One job per bigWig. The four jobs are independent and run in parallel; the
   legacy script read them one after another.
3. The joining rule needs all four. `expand()` with two lists gives
   rep1_plus, rep1_minus, rep2_plus, rep2_minus, in that order.
4. An output can be a list. In R it arrives as `snakemake@output$reps`.

```{.r filename="answers/snakemakeify/scripts/ttseq_signal.R"}
# Mean TT-seq coverage over each enhancer, for one replicate and one strand.
# Called by the ttseq_signal rule: one bigWig in, one TSV out.

log <- file(snakemake@log[[1]], open = "wt")
sink(log, type = "message")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicRanges)
  library(rtracklayer)
})

enhancers <- import(snakemake@input$enhancers)
cov <- import(snakemake@input$bigwig, as = "RleList")  # <1>

# one Views per chromosome, so this works for any chromosome in the GTF
means <- numeric(length(enhancers))
for (chrom in unique(as.character(seqnames(enhancers)))) {  # <2>
  idx <- which(seqnames(enhancers) == chrom)
  means[idx] <- Views(cov[[chrom]], ranges(enhancers[idx])) |>
    viewMeans() |>
    round(4)
}

data.frame(enhancer = enhancers$ID,
           chrom = as.character(seqnames(enhancers)),
           start = start(enhancers),
           end = end(enhancers),
           signal = means) |>
  write.table(snakemake@output[[1]], sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)  # <3>
```
1. The bigWig as per-base coverage, one `Rle` per chromosome.
2. The legacy script used `cov[["chr8"]]` directly. Looping over the
   chromosomes in the annotation means the same rule works for a genome-wide run.
3. One small table per bigWig, with a plain `signal` column. Which strand and
   replicate it is lives in the file name, where the wildcards put it.

```{.r filename="answers/snakemakeify/scripts/ttseq_tables.R"}
# Join the per-strand tables into one table per replicate (plus and minus
# columns), and stack the replicates into one combined table.
# Called by the ttseq_tables rule. Input order comes from expand():
# rep1_plus, rep1_minus, rep2_plus, rep2_minus.

log <- file(snakemake@log[[1]], open = "wt")
sink(log, type = "message")

reps    <- unlist(snakemake@params$reps)
strands <- unlist(snakemake@params$strands)
inputs  <- matrix(unlist(snakemake@input), nrow = length(strands),
                  dimnames = list(strands, reps))  # <1>

read_tsv <- \(f) read.delim(f, check.names = FALSE)

all_reps <- list()
for (i in seq_along(reps)) {
  per_strand <- lapply(strands, \(s) read_tsv(inputs[s, reps[i]]))
  tab <- per_strand[[1]][, c("enhancer", "chrom", "start", "end")]
  for (j in seq_along(strands)) {
    tab[[strands[j]]] <- per_strand[[j]]$signal
  }
  write.table(tab, snakemake@output$reps[[i]],  # <2>
              sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
  all_reps[[i]] <- cbind(rep = reps[i], tab)
}

do.call(rbind, all_reps) |>
  write.table(snakemake@output$combined, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```
1. Because `expand()` loops over the last list (strands) fastest, the inputs
   fill a strands x reps matrix column by column. `inputs["minus", "2"]` is
   replicate 2, minus strand.
2. The i-th file of the `reps` output list is replicate i's table.

**Check.** 6 jobs. All three tables (118 enhancers each, 236 rows in the
combined one) are byte-for-byte identical to the legacy output. A third
replicate is one more entry in `ttseq: reps:` and two more `ttseq_signal` jobs.

## Exercise S10: The whole of run_all.sh {#ex-s10}

`answers/snakemakeify/Snakefile` is every rule from S1-S9 in one file, with
the contents of `common.smk` at the top and this target rule:

```{.python filename="answers/snakemakeify/Snakefile (excerpt)"}
import pandas as pd


configfile: f"{workflow.basedir}/config.yaml"  # <1>

# ... samplesheet and sample lists, as in common.smk ...

rule all:  # <2>
    input:
        expand("results/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html", sample=SAMPLES),
        expand("results/tracks/{sample}.bw", sample=SAMPLES),  # <3>
        "results/qc/qc_summary.tsv",
        "results/sweep/sweep_counts.tsv",
        "results/overlap/counts.txt",
        "results/figures/MYC_locus.pdf",
        "results/ttseq/ttseq_enhancers_all.tsv",
```
1. `workflow.basedir` is the folder the Snakefile is in, so the config is found
   wherever you run from. A plain `configfile: "config.yaml"` is looked up in
   the folder you run Snakemake from.
2. `rule all` lists only the ends of the chains. The BAMs, peaks and index are
   pulled in because something on this list needs them. The order of the steps,
   which `run_all.sh` spelled out, is now worked out from the inputs and outputs.
3. The legacy filter step made a bigWig for every sample, controls included,
   but only the six peak samples feed the figure. To keep all ten, ask for them
   here. Leave this line out and Snakemake makes six.

**What changed compared with `run_all.sh`.**

| | `run_all.sh` | `Snakefile` |
|---|---|---|
| Step order | written by hand | from the inputs and outputs |
| A step fails | the next steps run anyway, on missing or empty files | Snakemake stops, deletes that job's outputs, and keeps the rest |
| Second run | 01-05 and 07 skip by file existence; 06, 08 and 09 always rerun (about 20 s) | `Nothing to be done` |
| An input changes | nothing notices | the jobs downstream of it rerun |
| Parallel | one command at a time | independent jobs side by side up to `-c` |
| Settings | at the top of nine files | `config.yaml` |

**Check.** In a fresh folder, `snakemake -s Snakefile -n` shows 91 jobs. The
real run with `-c 4` finished in 74 seconds; the legacy `run_all.sh` took 96
seconds. Every output matches the per-exercise runs. A second `-n` prints
`Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).` After
`touch results/filter/HCT116_CTCF_1.filt.bam`, the dry run shows 15 jobs:
the flagstat, bigWig and peaks of that sample, its four sweep jobs, and
everything that summarizes across samples (`sweep_counts`, `qc_summary`, the
three overlap rules, `consensus_peaks` for CTCF, `locus_plot`, `all`).

From here, the steps that turn this into a lab pipeline (a samplesheet and
config next to the launcher, `profiles/`, `envs/`, `workflows/rules/`, a dry-run
test) are the ones RegPipe takes in modules 5-8, and the ones the
[capstone](../capstone.qmd) asks for.
